source.title_on_document: Impact of LLM-Assisted Coding in Creativity and Robustness of Robot Controllers

supplement.holds: No separate supplement is cited. An Appendix inside this PDF (pp. 10-12) holds Figures 6-9 (DAT distribution, Normalized Compression Distance, coding experience, time to working result) and Table 1 (students' comments).

paper_design_summary: Thirteen male students from the University of Bologna Intelligent Robotic Systems course each wrote a simulated Foot-Bot path-following controller during a three-hour session. Seven used Microsoft Copilot and six coded without it; allocation balanced Divergent Association Task scores, and randomization was not reported. The authors compared controller performance, including under increased noise to simulate a pseudo-reality gap, and pairwise code similarity within each group using Dolos.

studies.label: Robot-controller coding with vs without Copilot (one course cohort)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Coding with Microsoft Copilot (with LLM) versus coding without it (without LLM)
assignment.quote: We use the test to divide the students in the two groups, maintaining as balanced as possible the distribution of the DAT score (see Figure 6).

arms.name: with LLM
arms.description: Coded the controller with Copilot available through its online interface (incognito); required to query Copilot at least three times; course material, lab code, and documentation allowed

arms.name: without LLM
arms.description: Coded the controller without LLM assistance; course materials, laboratory code, and simulation-environment and programming-language documentation were allowed. Internet access was prohibited except for those resources (p. 3, Section 3).

participants.who: Thirteen male University of Bologna students who attended the Intelligent Robotic Systems course; none reported work experience in robotics. The paper gives 7 and 6 per group and reports no exclusions.
participants.quote: The experiment involved thirteen male students, which we divided in two groups. Seven participants program with the assistance of LLMs, while the remaining six program without (see Figure 1).

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Copilot, May 2025 version, online interface in incognito mode (Quick Response and Think Deeper modes available)
ai_tool.how_used: Students in the LLM group had to query Copilot at least three times during development. Copilot saw only the code that students uploaded (p. 4, Section 3).

task.description: Write a Lua controller for a simulated Foot-Bot robot (ARGoS3 simulator) that searches for a black path and follows it as fast as possible; the evaluation function was shown to the students

outcomes.name: Pairwise code similarity within each group (Dolos plagiarism-detection software)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Dolos compares pairs of student controllers within each assistance group while ignoring comments, variable names, and text position (p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Figure 4). Appendix alternatives are Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) on raw code including comments and spaces and on corresponding Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs), using all two-student combinations within each group. All controllers contain common evaluation code (p. 10, Figure 7). Exact summary estimates and inferential tests are not reported.

contrasts.reported: Greater Dolos similarity with Copilot indicates lower diversity; the qualitative direction is reversed for the diversity construct, with no numerical effect calculated. The paper states: 'the code produced with the assistance of Copilot is significantly more similar that the one produced by the students alone (see Figure 4).' Exact arm medians and numerical effect estimates are not reported. Figure 4 has axis ticks but no printed median values. No test procedure, test statistic, p-value, or confidence interval is reported despite the narrative word 'significantly'. Appendix Figure 7 (p. 10) presents alternative Normalized Compression Distance measures on raw code and abstract syntax trees as box plots only, with no exact summary estimates or tests.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 4 (Results), second paragraph; p. 6, Figure 4; p. 10, Figure 7

diversity_detail.metric: Dolos pairwise code similarity (p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Figure 4). Appendix alternatives: Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) on raw code and corresponding Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) (p. 10, Figure 7).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: No embedding model is reported for these code-comparison measures.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Pairs of controllers produced by different students within each assistance group (p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Figure 4). The NCD caption explicitly specifies all combinations of two students within each group (p. 10, Figure 7). The paper does not print pair counts; n_units remains null.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not reported: no inferential test procedure, test statistic, p-value, standard error, or confidence interval is provided. The word 'significantly' appears in the Dolos results narrative without a supporting test (p. 5, Section 4).
diversity_detail.notes: Dolos ignores comments, variable names, and text position. The NCD alternatives compare raw code including comments and spaces and corresponding ASTs; the authors state that all controllers contain common evaluation code (p. 10, Figure 7). Figures 4 and 7 provide no exact summary estimates or tests. Greater Dolos similarity is coded as lower diversity; only the qualitative direction is reversed, and no numerical effect is calculated.

outcomes.name: Controller performance in simulation (Equation 1 evaluation function, 100 runs per arena; 3 training arenas and 2 test arenas, each at 1x and 5x noise as a pseudo-reality gap)
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Mixed, figure only (no numbers or tests printed). Text: 'The group coding without the assistance of the LLM obtained averagely better results in all the arenas. However, the group using Copilot attained the highest performance in the arenas presented to the students'. Under 5x noise 'the performances attained by the group using Copilot drop, while the performances obtained by the other group remain overall stable.'
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 4 (Results), first paragraph

eligibility.reason: The authors used Divergent Association Task scores to balance the assistance groups, but do not report whether allocation involved randomization (p. 4, Section 3; p. 5, Section 4; p. 10, Figure 6), so criterion 1 is unclear. Only 13 people took part, 7 with LLM and 6 without (p. 3, Section 3), so criterion 2 is not met and core eligibility remains no. Code similarity is computed on the controllers the students produced, so criterion 3 is met (p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Figure 4), although robot-controller programming is a borderline creative task. The comparison is retained as observational context; no randomized people study is documented. Self-reported coding experience and time (p. 11, Figures 8-9) are not output measures.

one_line_finding: Among 13 students (7 with Copilot, 6 without; p. 3, Section 3) in groups balanced on DAT scores with randomization unreported (p. 4, Section 3), controllers coded with Copilot were more similar within their group (Dolos, p. 6, Figure 4) and less robust to high noise (p. 5, Figure 3); both comparisons are figure only, with no numerical effect estimates or statistical tests printed.
